From Relevance to Validity: Zero-Shot Tool Selection via Functional and Contextual Validation

Xiaoxuan Dong Affiliation: UESTC    Jin Zhang Affiliation: LZU    Zichen Yuan Affiliation: CityUHK    Yue Zhou Affiliation: LZU    Zihao Rao Affiliation: CityUHK    Dexu Yu Affiliation: Northwestern    Tingyong Wu Affiliation: UESTC    Wenhao Deng Affiliation: UofG    Junchen Fu Affiliation: UofG    Pengwei Sun Affiliation: Stanford    Yang Ran Affiliation: Fenz AI    Bo Lan Affiliation: Fenz AI    Yongxin Ni Affiliation: NUS*Corresponding: youhuali2-c@my.cityu.edu.hk    Youhua Li Affiliation: CityUHK
Abstract

Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly face tasks from unseen domains and execution contexts, making zero-shot tool selection essential for identifying tools that can satisfy task requirements. Existing dominant methods mainly rely on relevance ranking, but semantic matching alone cannot ensure that a tool is functionally compatible or remains applicable in a new context. We preliminarily identify a transfer-validity gap, where semantically relevant tools may still fail to satisfy functional or contextual requirements after transfer. To address this gap, we propose TACT, a progressive validation framework that complements semantic relevance with endpoint-grounded functional compatibility and task-conditioned contextual evidence. Across cross-domain and cross-dataset transfer, TACT consistently improves capability ranking, with larger gains under functional or contextual ambiguity. Ablation results further confirm the complementary contributions of functional and contextual validation.

1 Introduction

As large language models increasingly interact with external tools, APIs, and services, agents must select suitable capabilities from growing libraries (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023). This problem becomes harder under distribution shift, where tasks may come from unseen domains or execution settings and target-side supervision is unavailable. Reliable zero-shot selection therefore requires transferring previously learned task–capability relations to new contexts.

Existing methods mainly improve candidate retrieval or ranking. Re-Invoke reformulates queries for zero-shot tool retrieval (Chen et al., 2024), while ToolRerank improves candidate ordering through adaptive reranking (Zheng et al., 2024). Other approaches extend selection through generation or open-world function calling (Wang et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025). These methods provide strong mechanisms for proposing plausible candidates, but relevance alone does not establish whether a candidate remains valid after transfer.

Two additional constraints arise. First, a relevant capability may lack an endpoint that jointly supports the required operation, arguments, and input types; semantic relevance therefore does not guarantee functional compatibility. Second, even a functionally valid capability may have been supported only under particular source-side conditions, such as platform, locale, access policy, or execution environment. Its contextual applicability must therefore be reassessed for the current task. As illustrated in Figure 1, zero-shot transfer must thus consider relevance, functional compatibility, and contextual applicability.

Preliminary controlled diagnostics reveal both gaps, as shown in Figure 2. Among eligible tasks, 44.25%44.25\% contain functionally different candidates with semantic scores less than 0.010.01 apart, indicating that semantic near-ties can mask functional incompatibility. Holding the capability and callable function fixed, changing only the task context reverses applicability in 15.20%15.20\% of determinate pairs with an applicable base context (62/40862/408). These diagnostics motivate progressive validation: semantic relevance proposes candidates, endpoint evidence evaluates functional compatibility, and task-conditioned source evidence assesses contextual applicability.

Based on this observation, we propose TACT, an evidence-grounded framework for zero-shot capability transfer. Semantic Proposal provides a frozen relevance anchor. Functional Validation scores task requirements against operation, argument, and type evidence composed within individual endpoints. Contextual Validation uses task-conditioned source evidence to adjust relations whose support changes across contexts. Finally, Validated Ranking combines these signals through bounded gates, retaining the preceding estimate when a correction has no supporting evidence.

We evaluate TACT under cross-domain and cross-dataset zero-shot transfer. TACT achieves the strongest aggregate ranking performance, with larger gains when semantically plausible candidates differ in functional compatibility or contextual applicability. On the cross-domain Context view, TACT improves NDCG@5 from 0.5180.518 for the strongest baseline, PORTS, to 0.6240.624. Ablation results confirm the contributions of both functional and contextual validation, while downstream execution shows corresponding gains in task completion across frozen agent backbones.

Our main contributions are:

  • •

    We identify the transfer-validity gap in zero-shot capability selection and distinguish semantic relevance, functional compatibility, and contextual applicability through controlled diagnostics.

  • •

    We introduce TACT, which performs progressive transfer validation through Semantic Proposal, Functional Validation, Contextual Validation, and Validated Ranking.

  • •

    We evaluate TACT across cross-domain and cross-dataset transfer, controlled candidate ambiguity, ablations, scaling, source-evidence availability, and frozen-agent execution.

2 Related Work

2.1 Tool Retrieval and Selection

API-Bank, TaskBench, StableToolBench, and ToolRet provide benchmarks for tool interaction, task automation, reproducible execution, and retrieval, respectively Li et al. (2023); Shen et al. (2024); Guo et al. (2024); Shi et al. (2025). Within this setting, selection methods differ in the evidence used to identify suitable candidates. ColBERTv2 captures fine-grained textual matches Santhanam et al. (2022); Re-Invoke and ToolDreamer enrich retrieval with synthetic queries or hypothetical tools Chen et al. (2024); Sengupta et al. (2026); and ToolRerank incorporates tool hierarchy and unseen-tool adaptation Zheng et al. (2024). PORTS further introduces downstream model preferences Molfetta et al. (2025), while task-aligned recommendation uses historical bundles to adjust toolset composition Gao and Zhang (2025). These signals improve candidate selection but do not explicitly score operation, argument, and type evidence within individual callable endpoints. TACT incorporates this structure in Functional Validation: requirement–endpoint matching aggregates evidence within each endpoint before assessing support for the task.

2.2 Transfer under Distribution Shift

Transfer methods differ in how they share information across domains. UniSRec learns reusable representations from item descriptions Hou et al. (2022), whereas AREAD adapts expert sharing to individual recommendation domains Luo et al. (2025). Domain-generalization methods constrain what should remain stable: Fishr aligns gradient variances across domains Rame et al. (2022), non-stationary generalization accounts for evolving domain patterns Pham et al. (2024), and sufficient invariant learning preserves predictive invariant information Kim et al. (2025). These approaches improve representation reuse or predictor robustness, but leave unresolved whether source evidence for a functionally compatible capability applies under the current task conditions. TACT therefore conditions source evidence on the current task and limits the magnitude of a signed contextual correction. This correction can increase or decrease a candidate’s score; its bound constrains the validation magnitude rather than imposing an upper bound on the final score. When evidence is unavailable, the correction vanishes and the gated functional estimate is retained.

3 Methodology

TACT follows a four-stage architecture: Semantic Proposal provides a relevance anchor, Functional Validation evaluates endpoint compatibility, Contextual Validation estimates task-conditioned applicability changes, and Validated Ranking combines these signals through bounded gates, as shown in Figure 3.

3.1 Problem Setup and Preliminary Diagnostics

Given a task tt in a held-out context d⋆d^{\star} and a candidate set 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t}, our goal is to rank capabilities without using target-side relevance labels for training, calibration, or model selection. We define the source records available for transfer

𝒮−d∗=⋃d≠d∗𝒮d.\mathcal{S}_{-d^{*}}=\bigcup_{d\neq d^{*}}\mathcal{S}_{d}. (1)

The model uses task and capability text, public endpoint schemas, and source-derived statistics, but receives neither target-context identity nor gold task decompositions.

We distinguish two transfer-validity gaps. Semantically similar candidates may differ in endpoint support for required operations and inputs, separating semantic relevance from functional compatibility. Functionally compatible capabilities may change applicability across task conditions, separating functional compatibility from contextual applicability.

Figure 2 measures these gaps independently of TACT. For functional ambiguity, we consider tasks whose frozen semantic Top-20 contains at least one clearly valid and one clearly invalid candidate. For each eligible task, we compute

dt=minc+∈𝒱t,c−∈ℐt⁡|ssem​(t,c+)−ssem​(t,c−)|,d_{t}=\min_{c^{+}\in\mathcal{V}_{t},\;c^{-}\in\mathcal{I}_{t}}\left|s_{\mathrm{sem}}(t,c^{+})-s_{\mathrm{sem}}(t,c^{-})\right|,

where 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t} and ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} denote functionally valid and invalid candidates. Among 29,178 eligible tasks, 44.25%44.25\% contain a functionally discordant pair with dt<0.01d_{t}<0.01, and 73.62%73.62\% do so with dt<0.05d_{t}<0.05.

For contextual instability, we construct outcome-blind minimal pairs that preserve the capability and callable function while changing one observed task-context condition. After blinded review and adjudication, 408 of 500 pairs have supported base tasks and determinate applicability labels; 62 flip and 346 remain stable, yielding a 15.20%15.20\% flip rate. These diagnostics motivate endpoint-grounded functional validation and selective contextual validation. They are excluded from training, calibration, and model selection; construction details and leakage controls appear in Appendix A.

Primary ranking evaluation uses four fixed candidate views—Natural, Semantic, Context, and Mixed—with a shared scorer, checkpoint, and calibration. Candidate construction and evaluation details appear in Appendices B and H.

3.2 Progressive Transfer Validation

Recent tool-retrieval methods identify plausible candidates through semantic retrieval or reranking (Chen et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024). TACT begins with a semantic task–capability relation. Endpoint evidence then assesses support for the required operations and inputs, while task-conditioned source evidence adjusts applicability under the current task conditions.

Validated Ranking.

Let A⁡(t,c)A(t,c) denote the frozen semantic anchor, I⁡(t,c)I(t,c) the functional compatibility score, and D⁡(t,c)D(t,c) the signed contextual correction. The final score combines them as

s⁡(t,c)=\displaystyle s(t,c)={} A⁡(t,c)\displaystyle A(t,c) (2)
+ωI​(t,c)​[I⁡(t,c)−A⁡(t,c)]\displaystyle+\omega_{I}(t,c)\bigl[I(t,c)-A(t,c)\bigr]
+ωD​(t,c)​D​(t,c).\displaystyle+\omega_{D}(t,c)D(t,c).

Here ωI,ωD∈[0,1]\omega_{I},\omega_{D}\in[0,1] are selected using source contexts only. The functional term interpolates between AA and II, while the contextual term adds a gated signed correction. When contextual evidence is unavailable, D⁡(t,c)=0D(t,c)=0 and the score reduces to the functional path.

Training objectives, gate parameterization, and optimization are detailed in Appendices C –F.

3.3 Endpoint-Grounded Functional Validation

Functional validation first refines the semantic retrieval proposal and then evaluates its support in the candidate’s documented endpoints. A frozen encoder E0E_{0} produces normalized task and capability representations ete_{t} and ece_{c}, from which we compute

a⁡(t,c)\displaystyle a(t,c) =⟨et,ec⟩−μaτa,\displaystyle=\frac{\langle e_{t},e_{c}\rangle-\mu_{a}}{\tau_{a}}, (3)
A⁡(t,c)\displaystyle A(t,c) =log⁡σ⁡(a⁡(t,c)).\displaystyle=\log\sigma\!\bigl(a(t,c)\bigr).

The parameters τa>0\tau_{a}>0 and μa\mu_{a} are calibrated on source data. The anchor preserves the cosine ranking and shares the log-sigmoid scale of the functional score.

Source-trained relation encoders produce normalized states zt,zcz_{t},z_{c} and a calibrated similarity b⁡(t,c)b(t,c). With δr​(t,c)=b⁡(t,c)−a⁡(t,c)\delta_{r}(t,c)=b(t,c)-a(t,c), we refine the semantic logit through a bounded residual:

Lrel​(t,c)=a⁡(t,c)+α​sr​tanh⁡(δr​(t,c)sr).L_{\mathrm{rel}}(t,c)=a(t,c)+\alpha s_{r}\tanh\!\left(\frac{\delta_{r}(t,c)}{s_{r}}\right). (4)

Setting α=0\alpha=0 recovers the semantic logit. We then refine LrelL_{\mathrm{rel}} through requirement–endpoint matching, combining operation, argument, and type evidence within each documented endpoint.

Endpoint-coherent requirement matching.

A deterministic task-only extractor produces a set of requirements 𝒩t={ni}i=1Mt\mathcal{N}_{t}=\{n_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M_{t}}. For capability cc, we retrieve a set of Kc≤KK_{c}\leq K deduplicated public endpoints shared across all requirements. For requirement ii and endpoint jj, let oi​jo_{ij}, ai​ja_{ij}, and yi​jy_{ij} denote operation, required-argument, and argument-type evidence. Availability masks mjam_{j}^{a} and mjym_{j}^{y} indicate whether the corresponding schema fields are present.

Evidence is composed within each endpoint before matching, with missing schema fields omitted from the weighted average:

vi​j=oi​j+λa​mja​ai​j+λy​mjy​yi​j1+λa​mja+λy​mjy.v_{ij}=\frac{o_{ij}+\lambda_{a}m_{j}^{a}a_{ij}+\lambda_{y}m_{j}^{y}y_{ij}}{1+\lambda_{a}m_{j}^{a}+\lambda_{y}m_{j}^{y}}. (5)

We search over partial one-to-one assignments X∈{0,1}Mt×KcX\in\{0,1\}^{M_{t}\times K_{c}}, where each requirement is matched to at most one endpoint and each endpoint is used at most once. We denote the feasible set by 𝒳=𝒳⁡(t,c)\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{X}(t,c). Unmatched requirements use a shared null score ν\nu. The resulting endpoint-set support is

Cws​(t,c)=\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{ws}}(t,c)={} 1MtmaxX∈𝒳[∑i,jXi​jvi​j\displaystyle\frac{1}{M_{t}}\max_{X\in\mathcal{X}}\Bigl[\sum_{i,j}X_{ij}v_{ij} (6)
+ν(Mt−|X|)].\displaystyle+\nu(M_{t}-|X|)\Bigr].

We calibrate Cws​(t,c)C_{\mathrm{ws}}(t,c) to zws​(t,c)z_{\mathrm{ws}}(t,c) and compare it with the relation logit. Let gws=zws−Lrelg_{\mathrm{ws}}=z_{\mathrm{ws}}-L_{\mathrm{rel}} and nX=|X⋆|n_{X}=|X^{\star}| for a maximizing assignment. This discrepancy determines the functional residual:

ΔI=ρws​{gws,nX>0,min⁡(gws,0),nX=0.\Delta_{I}=\rho_{\mathrm{ws}}\begin{cases}g_{\mathrm{ws}},&n_{X}>0,\\ \min(g_{\mathrm{ws}},0),&n_{X}=0.\end{cases} (7)

The reliability factor ρws\rho_{\mathrm{ws}} scales the residual according to the structural evidence, as defined in Appendix D.2. Missing requirements or endpoints give ρws=0\rho_{\mathrm{ws}}=0. When both are available but the assignment is all-null, we set ρws=1/2\rho_{\mathrm{ws}}=1/2 and retain a non-positive residual. We incorporate the residual through a bounded update:

ΓI​(t,c)=γI​sI​tanh⁡(ΔI​(t,c)sI).\Gamma_{I}(t,c)=\gamma_{I}s_{I}\tanh\!\left(\frac{\Delta_{I}(t,c)}{s_{I}}\right). (8)

During source-only training, semantic false friends provide an auxiliary endpoint-set ranking objective that separates candidates remaining close under semantic relevance. Reliability estimation, auxiliary supervision, and exact assignment search are detailed in Appendices D.1 and D.2.

3.4 Evidence-Bounded Contextual Validation

Contextual validation uses source profiles to adjust the functional estimate according to the conditions of the current task.

Positive source uses form a capability profile pcp_{c}, while the current task induces a soft mixture hth_{t} over source-context centroids. In cross-dataset transfer, source profiles are built from positive Natural-view records and indexed by dataset–capability pairs. A target capability obtains a profile by retrieving semantically similar source capabilities within each source dataset and combining their profiles using similarity and source-support weights. Semantic retrieval connects source and target capabilities across different IDs and names. The profile is set to zero when no source candidate exists or the maximum similarity is below 0.250.25. A centered low-rank transformation of (zc,pc,ht)(z_{c},p_{c},h_{t}) produces a task-conditioned capability state zcctx​(t)z_{c}^{\mathrm{ctx}}(t). We measure the resulting relation change as

Δ​r​(t,c)=⟨zt,zcctx​(t)⟩−⟨zt,zc⟩.\Delta r(t,c)=\langle z_{t},z_{c}^{\mathrm{ctx}}(t)\rangle-\langle z_{t},z_{c}\rangle. (9)

Selective contextual validation.

The applicability changes in Figure 2 motivate selective validation based on source confidence and observed task conditions. Let qconf​(t,c)q_{\mathrm{conf}}(t,c) measure confidence in the available source evidence and qshift​(t,c)q_{\mathrm{shift}}(t,c) measure task-observable context change:

ρctx​(t,c)=qconf​(t,c)​qshift​(t,c).\rho_{\mathrm{ctx}}(t,c)=q_{\mathrm{conf}}(t,c)q_{\mathrm{shift}}(t,c). (10)

This resembles selective prediction under distribution shift: uncertain cases retain the default estimate (Liang et al., 2024).

The contextual correction is

D⁡(t,c)=\displaystyle D(t,c)={} γD​ρctx​(t,c)​gev​(t,c)\displaystyle\gamma_{D}\rho_{\mathrm{ctx}}(t,c)g_{\mathrm{ev}}(t,c) (11)
×tanh⁡(Δ​r​(t,c)TD),\displaystyle\times\tanh\!\left(\frac{\Delta r(t,c)}{T_{D}}\right),

where gev∈[1−sg,1+sg]g_{\mathrm{ev}}\in[1-s_{g},1+s_{g}] calibrates evidence reliability, with 0≤sg≤10\leq s_{g}\leq 1, γD≥0\gamma_{D}\geq 0, and TD>0T_{D}>0. Because ρctx∈[0,1]\rho_{\mathrm{ctx}}\in[0,1], the correction satisfies |D⁡(t,c)|≤γD​(1+sg)|D(t,c)|\leq\gamma_{D}(1+s_{g}). Its sign follows Δ​r\Delta r, increasing or decreasing the score according to the change in task–capability alignment. All quantities use cross-fitted source evidence and task-observable information.

A neutrality loss discourages corrections for context-neutral tasks:

ℒneutral=𝔼⁡[(1−qshift​(t,c))​D​(t,c)2].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{neutral}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[(1-q_{\mathrm{shift}}(t,c))D(t,c)^{2}\right]. (12)

The regularization weight is largest when qshiftq_{\mathrm{shift}} is small and decreases as evidence of context change increases. Source confidence separately controls the correction through ρctx\rho_{\mathrm{ctx}}; absent source evidence gives ρctx=0\rho_{\mathrm{ctx}}=0 and hence D=0D=0.

Source profiles, context routing, reliability features, and optimization details are given in Appendices E –G.

3.5 Training and Model Selection

The two validation stages use supervision aligned with their respective failure modes. Functional validation uses ordinary negatives and semantic false friends, with the latter additionally supervising endpoint-set matching. Contextual validation uses contextual counterfactuals together with reliability and neutrality objectives that discourage unsupported corrections.

All model strengths, checkpoints, and fusion parameters are selected using source contexts only. After selection, the chosen configuration is retrained on the complete source set and evaluated once on the held-out target. For cross-dataset transfer, the scorer is unchanged; unlabeled target embedding statistics are used only for label-free coordinate alignment.

4 Experiments

  • •

    RQ1: Does TACT improve zero-shot capability ranking under semantic, contextual, and mixed transfer failures?

  • •

    RQ2: Do functional validation and contextual validation correct distinct transfer errors?

  • •

    RQ3: Do ranking gains improve execution completion across agent backbones?

  • •

    RQ4: Does TACT remain effective as capability libraries expand and source evidence becomes limited?

4.1 Experimental Setup

Transfer protocols.

Cross-domain transfer uses leave-one-domain-out evaluation over 49 ToolBench domains, with the other 48 providing source supervision. Cross-dataset transfer holds out each of ToolBench (Qin et al., 2024), TaskBench (Shen et al., 2024), MetaTool (Huang et al., 2024), and APIBench (Patil et al., 2024), using the other three as sources. These protocols assess within-benchmark generalization and broader shifts in task and capability distributions, respectively. Training, calibration, and model selection use source data only; cross-dataset transfer also uses unlabeled target embeddings for label-free coordinate alignment. Results are averaged over seeds 42, 43, and 44, then equally across scored targets.

Baselines and metrics.

Baselines include frozen retrieval (Random and Semantic Cosine), source-trained Pointwise MLP; transfer methods ZESRec (Ding et al., 2021), UniSRec (Hou et al., 2022), and AREAD (Luo et al., 2025); and tool-retrieval methods Re-Invoke (Chen et al., 2024), PORTS (Molfetta et al., 2025), and ToolDreamer (Sengupta et al., 2026). Endpoint Schema Match uses public endpoint and schema evidence, while MultiPool pools source data. Re-Invoke, ToolDreamer, and PORTS retain their original configurations under the shared ranking interface; PORTS uses the authors’ code. Backbones, encoders, and source-data use appear in Appendix I.3. We report MRR, NDCG@5, and HR@3; split statistics and implementation details appear in Appendices H and I.

4.2 Overall Performance (RQ1)

TACT achieves the highest aggregate scores across both transfer protocols, with larger NDCG@5 gains on the constructed views than on Natural. Table 1 shows the largest cross-domain improvement on Context, where NDCG@5 rises from 0.518 for PORTS to 0.624 for TACT. On Natural, where semantic retrieval is already strong, TACT improves NDCG@5 from 0.841 for ToolDreamer to 0.873.

The same pattern holds in cross-dataset transfer. On Mixed, TACT increases NDCG@5 from 0.463 for ToolDreamer to 0.500, compared with an increase from 0.733 for MultiPool to 0.746 on Natural. The larger improvement on Mixed indicates that validation is especially useful when the candidate set combines functional and contextual ambiguity.

TACT also improves on retrieval using the same public schema evidence. On cross-domain Semantic, it achieves NDCG@5 of 0.604, compared with 0.547 for Endpoint Schema Match, the strongest baseline on this metric. This comparison supports combining endpoint evidence with learned task–capability relations and contextual validation. Per-target Full-model results and held-out-group comparisons appear in Appendices J.2 and J.3.

4.3 Validation-Stage Analysis (RQ2)

The full model performs best across both protocols, with functional validation contributing broadly and contextual validation having a more selective effect. Table 2 compares variants trained and selected independently using source data.

Removing functional validation reduces cross-domain NDCG@5 by 0.059 on Semantic, 0.067 on Context, and 0.062 on Mixed. Its contribution persists across datasets, where removal lowers NDCG@5 by 0.048 on Mixed. Contextual validation contributes most on cross-domain Context and Mixed. Removing it lowers NDCG@5 by 0.072 and 0.046, compared with 0.020 on Natural and 0.012 on Semantic. Its effect is smaller in cross-dataset transfer, where the reductions are 0.016 on Natural, 0.002 on Semantic, 0.009 on Context, and 0.003 on Mixed. The contextual contribution therefore depends more strongly on the transfer setting.

4.4 Downstream Cached Execution (RQ3)

TACT achieves the highest task completion rate across all four frozen agent backbones. Figure 4 reports results on 120 solvable StableToolBench queries under cached execution.

Compared with Re-Invoke, the strongest competing selector, completion increases from 20.83% to 29.17% on GPT-5.6 Terra, from 14.17% to 22.50% on Grok-4.5, from 12.50% to 20.83% on Claude Sonnet 5, and from 17.50% to 26.67% on Gemini 3.1 Pro. All retrieval policies select the top five capabilities from the same 3,442-capability library and use identical queries and execution budgets. Ranking configurations and agent policies remain fixed throughout evaluation. Under these shared conditions, the completion gains show that improved capability selection benefits downstream execution across different agent models.

4.5 Scalability and Limits of Transfer Validation (RQ4)

RQ4 uses the primary experiment’s Full checkpoints and shared calibration.

Candidate-library scaling.

TACT remains ahead of Semantic Cosine as the candidate library grows. Table 3 expands the ToolBench library from the base setting to all 3,442 capabilities. At full scale, NDCG@5 is 0.401 versus 0.382 on Natural and 0.260 versus 0.056 on Context. Both methods lose accuracy as more candidates compete for the top ranks, while TACT’s advantage remains larger on Semantic, Context, and Mixed. Cross-dataset results and candidate-pool definitions appear in Appendix L.

Source-evidence availability.

The contextual contribution grows with retained source evidence, most clearly on Context and Mixed. Figure 5 varies source associations while holding model parameters, outer splits, candidate pools, and calibration fixed. Each checkpoint is shared across the four candidate views. The comparator, Fixed-Checkpoint Functional Fallback, removes the contextual contribution from the same checkpoint, allowing its ranking contribution to be measured at each evidence level. Full and fallback coincide at zero evidence. Further comparator details appear in Appendix L.

5 Conclusion

We presented TACT for zero-shot capability transfer, refining semantic relevance through Endpoint-Grounded Functional Validation and Evidence-Bounded Contextual Validation. Across cross-domain and cross-dataset evaluations, TACT improves aggregate capability ranking, with larger gains on candidate sets containing functional or contextual ambiguity. These gains also translate into higher task completion rates across four frozen agent backbones under cached execution. The results support combining semantic relevance with functional compatibility and contextual applicability for capability selection.

Acknowledgement

The work described in this paper was partially supported by InnoHK initiative, The Government of the HKSAR, and Laboratory for AI-Powered Financial Technologies.

Limitations

Our evaluation uses fixed capability libraries and held-out domain or dataset splits. The reported ranking gains therefore do not establish performance for newly added capabilities, changing endpoint schemas, or live services. The closed-world relevance annotations treat unjudged candidates as non-relevant in expanded pools, so the scaling results measure recovery of known positives rather than complete compatibility assessment. The cached execution study uses a fixed set of solvable queries and frozen agent backbones; its completion rates may not transfer to unrestricted tasks, live API failures, or other agents. Contextual applicability also depends on source association evidence and falls back through the gated functional path when that evidence is unavailable.

Appendix A ToolBench Motivating Diagnostic Details

This appendix specifies the two diagnostics in Figure 2 of the main paper: functional ambiguity under frozen semantic retrieval and contextual instability under a minimal change to task conditions. These diagnostics characterize the transfer-validity gaps motivating TACT; they are not evaluations of the full ranking model.

A.1 Diagnostic Scope and Isolation

The functional diagnostic uses frozen semantic scores and public capability and endpoint information. The contextual diagnostic uses outcome-blind minimal pairs followed by blinded review and adjudication. Diagnostic annotations and outcomes are not used to train, calibrate, select, or tune TACT. These diagnostics answer different questions from the candidate audits in Appendix H.4; their denominators must not be combined.

A.2 Functional Ambiguity in Semantic Retrieval

For task tt, let 𝒞t20\mathcal{C}^{20}_{t} be its frozen semantic Top-20 candidate set. Within this set, 𝒱t\mathcal{V}_{t} and ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} denote candidates with clear functionally valid and invalid labels, respectively. A task is eligible only if both sets are nonempty. Unresolved candidates do not establish eligibility. Functional validity concerns whether the callable interface supports the required operation and inputs.

For each eligible task, define the smallest semantic separation between functionally discordant candidates:

dt=minc+∈𝒱tc−∈ℐt⁡|ssem​(t,c+)−ssem​(t,c−)|.\displaystyle d_{t}=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}c^{+}\in\mathcal{V}_{t}\\ c^{-}\in\mathcal{I}_{t}\end{subarray}}\bigl|s_{\mathrm{sem}}(t,c^{+})-s_{\mathrm{sem}}(t,c^{-})\bigr|. (13)

Here ssems_{\mathrm{sem}} is the frozen semantic score, before the learned functional or contextual corrections. If 𝒯elig\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{elig}} is the eligible task set, the ambiguity rate at threshold ϵ\epsilon is

Ramb(ϵ)=1|𝒯elig|∑t∈𝒯elig𝕀[dt<ϵ].R_{\mathrm{amb}}(\epsilon)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{elig}}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{elig}}}\mathbb{I}[d_{t}<\epsilon]. (14)

The denominator is 29,178 eligible tasks. Table 4 reproduces the thresholds and rates in the main-text diagnostic. These are task-level ambiguity rates, not ranking accuracies or domain-macro averages.

A.3 Contextual Instability under Minimal Changes

Each minimal pair ((t(0),c),(t(1),c))((t^{(0)},c),(t^{(1)},c)) preserves the capability and callable function while changing one observed task-context condition. The pair is constructed without conditioning on whether applicability will flip. This avoids defining a diagnostic population consisting only of successful counterfactual flips.

Two automated judges assessed all 500 pairs independently: 324 received clear agreement and 176 underwent follow-up review and author adjudication. Judgments used task texts, capability descriptions, endpoint schemas, and context values. TACT scores and expected flip outcomes were excluded from the judgment evidence. This protocol uses automated assessment with author adjudication, rather than two independent human annotations.

Let 𝒫valid\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{valid}} contain pairs whose base task is supported and whose applicability is determinate on both sides. With yj(0),yj(1)∈{0,1}y_{j}^{(0)},y_{j}^{(1)}\in\{0,1\} denoting the final applicability labels, the conditional flip rate is

Rflip=∑j∈𝒫valid𝕀[yj(0)≠yj(1)]|𝒫valid|.R_{\mathrm{flip}}=\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{valid}}}\mathbb{I}[y_{j}^{(0)}\neq y_{j}^{(1)}]}{|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{valid}}|}. (15)

Of the 500 constructed pairs, 408 meet this criterion: 62 flip and 346 remain stable, yielding 62/408=15.20%62/408=15.20\% and 346/408=84.80%346/408=84.80\%, respectively. The other 54 pairs have unsupported base tasks and 38 remain indeterminate; neither category is counted as stable.

The reported 95% cluster-bootstrap interval for the flip rate is 11.57–19.09%. It uses 20,000 replicates with seed 20261012, resampling 333 clusters defined by capability name and changed context type. Table 5 disaggregates the included pairs by the changed context condition.

A.4 Interpretation and Scope

Functional ambiguity demonstrates that semantic near-ties can conceal different endpoint-level validity. Contextual instability demonstrates that applicability can change even when the capability and callable function remain fixed. Together, they motivate requirement–endpoint matching and selective contextual adjustment. Neither rate estimates the accuracy of an endpoint probe or the benefit of a learned correction.

Appendix B Task Construction and Endpoint Preprocessing

B.1 Negative Roles and Candidate Manifests

Each source negative candidate is assigned one of three roles: ordinary, semantic, or contextual. Positive candidates retain their positive labels. Ordinary negatives are generally irrelevant candidates. Semantic negatives are topically related but violate an operation, required-input, schema, or functional-boundary requirement. Contextual negatives remain functionally plausible but are unsupported under the relevant source context.

Contextual negatives are excluded from functional-relation training. Ordinary and semantic negatives are used as controls for contextual adjustment. In primary ranking experiments, Natural, Semantic, Context, and Mixed modify only the candidate set 𝒞t(v)\mathcal{C}_{t}^{(v)}; all views share the same scorer, parameters, gates, and calibration.

B.2 Task-Requirement Extraction

A deterministic task-only extractor splits a task into action clauses, attaches local constraints, merges near-duplicates, and retains at most Nmax=4N_{\max}=4 requirements. It reads task text only and never accesses candidate schemas, source labels, gold endpoints, or target annotations. The same requirement set is reused for every candidate.

For requirement nin_{i}, frozen query vectors are built for operation, required-argument, and argument-type evidence:

qir\displaystyle q_{i}^{r} =E0​(πr⊕ni),\displaystyle=E_{0}(\pi_{r}\oplus n_{i}), (16)
r\displaystyle r ∈{op,arg,type}.\displaystyle\in\{\mathrm{op},\mathrm{arg},\mathrm{type}\}.

These are the endpoint-evidence views used in Section 3.3 of the main paper.

B.3 Endpoint Preprocessing

Endpoint rows are deduplicated using the capability identifier, operation name, description, HTTP method, required argument names, and required argument types. For each candidate we retain a shared Top-KK endpoint set for all functional evidence channels, with K=4K=4 in the reported configuration. This is one shared set per task–capability pair, rather than a separate Top-KK set for each requirement. All requirements and evidence channels use this same set. Availability masks mjam_{j}^{a} and mjym_{j}^{y} indicate whether required-argument and argument-type schema fields are present. Missing fields provide no evidence and are not interpreted as mismatches.

B.4 Nested Source-Only Selection

For each outer target, complete source contexts are held out internally for checkpoint and strength selection, as detailed in Appendix G. When a context is used for source validation, all of its observations are excluded from capability profiles, support statistics, and task-conditioned source mixtures. After selection, the chosen configuration is retrained on the complete outer-source set and applied once to the unseen target.

Appendix C Relational Compatibility Objective

The frozen encoder E0E_{0} gives normalized task and capability vectors et,ece_{t},e_{c}, and the source-trained relation encoders give normalized states zt,zcz_{t},z_{c}. The semantic and relational logits are

a⁡(t,c)\displaystyle a(t,c) =⟨et,ec⟩−μaτa,\displaystyle=\frac{\langle e_{t},e_{c}\rangle-\mu_{a}}{\tau_{a}}, (17)
b⁡(t,c)\displaystyle b(t,c) =⟨zt,zc⟩−μrτr.\displaystyle=\frac{\langle z_{t},z_{c}\rangle-\mu_{r}}{\tau_{r}}.

The frozen anchor and bounded relational refinement are

A⁡(t,c)\displaystyle A(t,c) =log⁡σ⁡(a⁡(t,c)),\displaystyle=\log\sigma(a(t,c)), (18)
Lrel​(t,c)\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{rel}}(t,c) =a⁡(t,c)+α​sr\displaystyle=a(t,c)+\alpha s_{r}
×tanh⁡(b⁡(t,c)−a⁡(t,c)sr).\displaystyle\times\tanh\!\left(\frac{b(t,c)-a(t,c)}{s_{r}}\right).

All calibration temperatures are positive and fitted or selected using source data only. This reproduces Equations (3)–(4) of the main paper. Setting α=0\alpha=0 recovers the semantic logit; applying log⁡σ\log\sigma then recovers the anchor score.

ℓrel=\displaystyle\ell_{\mathrm{rel}}={} softplus⁡(mrel−Lrel​(t,c+)CLOSE\displaystyle\operatorname{softplus}\!\Bigl(m_{\mathrm{rel}}-L_{\mathrm{rel}}(t,c^{+}) (19)

wff=σ⁡(⟨et,ec−⟩−⟨et,ec+⟩Tff).w_{\mathrm{ff}}=\sigma\!\left(\frac{\langle e_{t},e_{c^{-}}\rangle-\langle e_{t},e_{c^{+}}\rangle}{T_{\mathrm{ff}}}\right). (20)

The complete relation objective combines source-only pairwise supervision with the false-friend term and the regularizers used by the relation encoder:

Here ℛrel\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{rel}} collects the pointwise, representation-margin, cross-context consistency, and anchor-preservation terms. Contextual counterfactuals are not used as negatives for this stage.

Appendix E Contextual Validation Details

E.1 Source Profiles and Task Context

Let μk\mu_{k} be the normalized task centroid of source context kk, and let nc,kn_{c,k} count distinct positive uses of capability cc in that context. The capability profile and task-conditioned source mixture are

pc\displaystyle p_{c} =norm⁡(∑klog⁡(1+nc,k)​μk∑klog⁡(1+nc,k)+ϵ),\displaystyle=\operatorname{norm}\!\left(\frac{\sum_{k}\log(1+n_{c,k})\mu_{k}}{\sum_{k}\log(1+n_{c,k})+\epsilon}\right), (35)
αk​(t)\displaystyle\alpha_{k}(t) =exp⁡(⟨et,μk⟩/τctx)∑jexp⁡(⟨et,μj⟩/τctx),\displaystyle=\frac{\exp(\langle e_{t},\mu_{k}\rangle/\tau_{\mathrm{ctx}})}{\sum_{j}\exp(\langle e_{t},\mu_{j}\rangle/\tau_{\mathrm{ctx}})},
ht\displaystyle h_{t} =norm⁡(∑kαk​(t)​μk).\displaystyle=\operatorname{norm}\!\left(\sum_{k}\alpha_{k}(t)\mu_{k}\right).

When a source context is held out for inner validation, it is excluded from all centroids, profiles, and routing statistics.

Cross-dataset profile transfer.

Source capability identity is the pair (s,cs)(s,c_{s}), where ss denotes a source dataset and csc_{s} its local capability ID. For each pair, positive records in the source dataset’s Natural view identify the task domains in which that capability is used. These records are aggregated into a distribution over contextual prototypes. The profile bank contains only source datasets; the held-out target dataset contributes no positive records to it. Shared capability IDs and normalized-name matching are not required.

To score a target capability cc, its embedding retrieves the most similar source capability profiles within each source dataset. The retrieved profiles are combined with weights reflecting embedding similarity and source-support strength. The resulting distribution provides the transferred context profile and its source-support evidence. If no source candidate exists, or the highest similarity is below 0.250.25, the transferred profile is zero. Otherwise, a capability with a new target-side ID can inherit evidence from semantically similar source capabilities. Such evidence remains source-derived; embedding similarity does not create target-positive observations.

E.2 Cross-Fitted Evidence Confidence

Support strength and source-context coverage are

qstr​(c)\displaystyle q_{\mathrm{str}}(c) =min⁡(1,log⁡(1+∑knc,k)log⁡N0),\displaystyle=\min\!\left(1,\frac{\log(1+\sum_{k}n_{c,k})}{\log N_{0}}\right), (36)
qcov​(c)\displaystyle q_{\mathrm{cov}}(c) =min(1,|{k:nc,k>0}|K0),\displaystyle=\min\!\left(1,\frac{|\{k:n_{c,k}>0\}|}{K_{0}}\right),
qsup​(c)\displaystyle q_{\mathrm{sup}}(c) =qstr​(c)​qcov​(c).\displaystyle=\sqrt{q_{\mathrm{str}}(c)q_{\mathrm{cov}}(c)}.

Routing confidence is

qroute​(t)=1−H⁡(α⁡(t))log⁡Kt,q_{\mathrm{route}}(t)=1-\frac{H(\alpha(t))}{\log K_{t}}, (37)

where Kt>1K_{t}>1 is the number of available source contexts. The expression is evaluated only when that condition holds; absent source evidence disables the contextual correction. In the main-text notation,

qconf​(t,c)=qsup​(c)​qroute​(t).q_{\mathrm{conf}}(t,c)=\sqrt{q_{\mathrm{sup}}(c)\,q_{\mathrm{route}}(t)}. (38)

When neither an observed source-positive profile nor an admissible transferred source profile is available, set pc=0p_{c}=0 and qsup​(c)=0q_{\mathrm{sup}}(c)=0, disabling contextual correction. In cross-dataset transfer, this condition is evaluated after semantic profile retrieval, not by testing whether the target capability ID appears in a source dataset. Coordinate alignment alone supplies no positive source-use evidence.

E.3 Centered Task-Conditioned Dynamics

Let μ¯src\bar{\mu}_{\mathrm{src}} be the normalized mean source centroid. The centered context code is

vctx​(t)=EΔ​(ht)−EΔ​(μ¯src).v_{\mathrm{ctx}}(t)=E_{\Delta}(h_{t})-E_{\Delta}(\bar{\mu}_{\mathrm{src}}). (39)

A low-rank operator gives

δ0​(t,c)=U⁡[G⁡(vctx​(t))⊙V​zc].\delta_{0}(t,c)=U\!\left[G(v_{\mathrm{ctx}}(t))\odot Vz_{c}\right]. (40)

We remove the component parallel to zcz_{c},

δ⟂​(t,c)=δ0​(t,c)−⟨δ0​(t,c),zc⟩​zc.\delta_{\perp}(t,c)=\delta_{0}(t,c)-\langle\delta_{0}(t,c),z_{c}\rangle z_{c}. (41)

The source profile contributes a second tangent direction,

uc\displaystyle u_{c} =tanh⁡(Ause​(pc)),\displaystyle=\tanh\!\left(A_{\mathrm{use}}(p_{c})\right), (42)
uc,⟂\displaystyle u_{c,\perp} =uc−⟨uc,zc⟩​zc.\displaystyle=u_{c}-\langle u_{c},z_{c}\rangle z_{c}.

Define the task-observable context activity

qshift​(t,c)≡actx​(t)=‖ht−μ¯src‖2‖ht−μ¯src‖2+1,q_{\mathrm{shift}}(t,c)\equiv a_{\mathrm{ctx}}(t)=\frac{\|h_{t}-\bar{\mu}_{\mathrm{src}}\|_{2}}{\|h_{t}-\bar{\mu}_{\mathrm{src}}\|_{2}+1}, (43)

and

Bound⁡(x)=x‖x‖2+τdev,\operatorname{Bound}(x)=\frac{x}{\|x\|_{2}+\tau_{\mathrm{dev}}}, (44)

where τdev>0\tau_{\mathrm{dev}}>0 is a smoothing constant that keeps the mapping well-defined at x=0x=0 and ensures ‖Bound⁡(x)‖2<1\|\operatorname{Bound}(x)\|_{2}<1. The contextual deviation and task-conditioned capability state are

δ⁡(t,c)=\displaystyle\delta(t,c)={} δ⟂​(t,c)+ηuse​qshift​(t,c)\displaystyle\delta_{\perp}(t,c)+\eta_{\mathrm{use}}q_{\mathrm{shift}}(t,c) (45)
×Bound⁡(uc,⟂),\displaystyle\times\operatorname{Bound}(u_{c,\perp}),
zcctx​(t)=\displaystyle z_{c}^{\mathrm{ctx}}(t)={} norm⁡(zcCLOSE\displaystyle\operatorname{norm}\!\Bigl(z_{c}
OPEN+κ​Bound⁡(δ⁡(t,c))).\displaystyle+\kappa\operatorname{Bound}(\delta(t,c))\Bigr).

The relation change in Equation (9) of the main paper is

Δ​r​(t,c)=⟨zt,zcctx​(t)⟩−⟨zt,zc⟩.\Delta r(t,c)=\langle z_{t},z_{c}^{\mathrm{ctx}}(t)\rangle-\langle z_{t},z_{c}\rangle. (46)

Here qshiftq_{\mathrm{shift}} is a task-observable context-activity proxy. Although written as a task–capability quantity for consistency with the main text, this parameterization depends on the task alone. It is not a target-context identifier or a directly observed applicability-flip label.

E.4 Selective Reliability and Evidence Calibration

The selective reliability in the main paper is therefore

ρctx​(t,c)=qconf​(t,c)​qshift​(t,c).\rho_{\mathrm{ctx}}(t,c)=q_{\mathrm{conf}}(t,c)q_{\mathrm{shift}}(t,c). (47)

The evidence gate uses source-support, routing, and relation features:

gev​(t,c)=1+sg​tanh⁡(MLPD⁡(xD)).g_{\mathrm{ev}}(t,c)=1+s_{g}\tanh\!\left(\operatorname{MLP}_{D}(x_{D})\right). (48)

For 0≤sg≤10\leq s_{g}\leq 1, the gate lies in [1−sg,1+sg][1-s_{g},1+s_{g}]. Its final layer is zero-initialized, so gev=1g_{\mathrm{ev}}=1 before contextual training.

The contextual correction is

D⁡(t,c)=\displaystyle D(t,c)={} γD​ρctx​(t,c)​gev​(t,c)\displaystyle\gamma_{D}\rho_{\mathrm{ctx}}(t,c)g_{\mathrm{ev}}(t,c) (49)
×tanh⁡(Δ​r​(t,c)TD),\displaystyle\times\tanh\!\left(\frac{\Delta r(t,c)}{T_{D}}\right),

with γD≥0\gamma_{D}\geq 0 and TD>0T_{D}>0, matching Equation (11). Since 0≤ρctx≤10\leq\rho_{\mathrm{ctx}}\leq 1, the magnitude is bounded by |D⁡(t,c)|≤γD​(1+sg)|D(t,c)|\leq\gamma_{D}(1+s_{g}). The correction vanishes when source confidence or task-observable context activity is zero. Otherwise, its sign follows Δ​r\Delta r.

The neutrality penalty in the main paper is exactly

ℒneutral=𝔼⁡[(1−qshift​(t,c))​D​(t,c)2].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{neutral}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[(1-q_{\mathrm{shift}}(t,c))D(t,c)^{2}\right]. (50)

E.5 Contextual Training Objective

For a context-supported positive c+c^{+} and a contextual counterfactual c−c^{-}, we use

ℒcf=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cf}}={} 𝔼[softplus(mD−D(t,c+)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\Bigl[\operatorname{softplus}\!\Bigl(m_{D}-D(t,c^{+}) (51)
+D(t,c−))].\displaystyle+D(t,c^{-})\Bigr)\Bigr].

Positive stability discourages negative corrections on supported positives; ordinary and semantic negatives act as controls against spurious contextual corrections. The neutrality objective in Equation 50 is included to discourage changes on context-neutral tasks. Fusion losses are defined in Appendix F and use source pairs only.

Appendix F Validated Ranking and Analysis Variants

The reported scorer uses a shared dual-gate fusion network. Its input contains the source-derived context feature vector together with compact relation summaries: the bounded relational residual, semantic cosine, relational cosine, functional relation score, contextual correction, source-evidence confidence, and context activity. No candidate-view identifier is provided.

The network produces logits ℓI\ell_{I} and ℓD\ell_{D}. For b∈{I,D}b\in\{I,D\}, the suppress-only gate is

hb=tanh⁡(ℓb),ωb=1−hb+|hb|2.h_{b}=\tanh(\ell_{b}),\qquad\omega_{b}=1-\frac{h_{b}+|h_{b}|}{2}. (52)

Thus ωI,ωD∈[0,1]\omega_{I},\omega_{D}\in[0,1]. The final score is

s⁡(t,c)=\displaystyle s(t,c)={} A⁡(t,c)\displaystyle A(t,c) (53)
+ωI​(t,c)​[I⁡(t,c)−A⁡(t,c)]\displaystyle+\omega_{I}(t,c)[I(t,c)-A(t,c)]
+ωD​(t,c)​D​(t,c),\displaystyle+\omega_{D}(t,c)D(t,c),

matching Equation (2) of the main paper. “Suppress-only” refers to the amplitudes of these gates. It does not constrain DD to be non-positive and does not imply s⁡(t,c)≤I⁡(t,c)s(t,c)\leq I(t,c).

If D=0D=0, the final score recovers the gated functional path

sfb​(t,c)=A⁡(t,c)+ωI​(t,c)​[I⁡(t,c)−A⁡(t,c)].s_{\mathrm{fb}}(t,c)=A(t,c)+\omega_{I}(t,c)[I(t,c)-A(t,c)]. (54)

This is equal to II only when the functional gate is one (or I=AI=A). If both corrections are disabled, the score recovers AA.

For an algebraic removal from Equation (53) that preserves the other gate, the two paths are

sno​ctx\displaystyle s_{\mathrm{no\ ctx}} =A+ωI​(I−A),\displaystyle=A+\omega_{I}(I-A), (55)
sno​func\displaystyle s_{\mathrm{no\ func}} =A+ωD​D.\displaystyle=A+\omega_{D}D.

The raw branch scores II and A+DA+D generally differ from these gate-preserving diagnostic scores. Neither raw branch scores nor fixed-checkpoint removals are equivalent to independently trained branch ablations: retraining can change the retained parameters, calibration, and selected checkpoint. Primary ranking configurations are selected using source data and shared across candidate views. The anchor-only variant uses the same frozen task and capability representations as Semantic Cosine. Because A⁡(t,c)A(t,c) is a monotonic calibration of the cosine score, the two induce identical rankings.

F.1 Fusion Supervision

For a source pair (c+,c−)(c^{+},c^{-}), the fused ranking loss is

ℒF=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{F}={} 𝔼[softplus(mF−s(t,c+)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\Bigl[\operatorname{softplus}\!\Bigl(m_{F}-s(t,c^{+}) (56)
+s(t,c−))].\displaystyle+s(t,c^{-})\Bigr)\Bigr].

Fusion training also uses a source-only dominance term that prevents the fused margin from falling below the stronger branch margin, a routing loss that supervises gate suppression from relative source-side branch margins, and a gate regularizer that keeps both gates near the unsuppressed state unless source evidence supports suppression. No target labels or view identifiers enter these losses.

Appendix G Source-Only Optimization and Model Selection

G.1 Staged Objectives

The frozen text encoder is never updated. Source-only optimization first fits the anchor-preserving relational refinement in Appendix C. Endpoint-set parameters are trained with the functional objective in Appendix D.2, while contextual and fusion parameters use the objectives in Appendices E–F. The preceding relation path is held fixed during the corresponding refinement stages. Ordinary negatives and semantic false friends supervise functional validity; contextual counterfactuals supervise contextual applicability.

G.2 Nested Source-Only Selection

For each outer target, complete source contexts are held out internally. Their observations are excluded from the centroids, capability profiles, support statistics, and routing evidence used to score those contexts. Checkpoints, calibration parameters, residual strengths, and fusion settings are selected on these held-out source contexts. Correction-strength grids include zero to permit fallback when additional evidence does not improve source validation.

After selection, the chosen configuration is retrained on the complete outer-source set and evaluated once on the held-out target. Primary ranking and independently trained branch ablations share each selected configuration across Natural, Semantic, Context, and Mixed; the view identifier is not a scorer input. The source-evidence diagnostic uses the same Full checkpoints and shared calibration as the primary ranking experiment, as detailed in Appendix L. Numerical settings are consolidated in Appendix I.

G.3 Shared Functional and Contextual Modes

Both transfer protocols use at most four task requirements, one shared Top-4 endpoint set, within-endpoint operation/argument/type composition, exact partial injective assignment, a bounded functional residual, selective contextual reliability, and two bounded fusion gates. These mechanisms are unchanged across candidate views.

G.4 Cross-Dataset Label-Free Coordinate Alignment

Cross-domain and cross-dataset experiments use the same scorer architecture. Before cross-dataset scoring, task and capability embeddings are statistically aligned using each dataset’s own unlabeled means and standard deviations. This includes the held-out target’s unlabeled statistics and is therefore transductive preprocessing. Target relevance labels are excluded from model fitting, calibration, early stopping, checkpoint selection, and source-profile construction. The target dataset remains excluded from the source-profile bank.

Appendix H Evaluation Protocol Statistics and Candidate Audits

This appendix complements the evaluation protocol in Section 4 of the main paper with the exact outer splits, domain-level coverage, candidate-manifest statistics, and independent candidate audits. We additionally clarify the evaluation boundary and the controls used to prevent target-side information from influencing model development.

H.1 Outer Splits and Result Aggregation

Cross-domain evaluation uses leave-one-domain-out (LODO) transfer over the 49 ToolBench domains. Each target domain is held out once, and the other 48 domains provide source data. Cross-dataset evaluation holds out one of ToolBench, TaskBench, MetaTool, and APIBench, using the other three datasets as sources. Training, calibration, checkpoint selection, and early stopping use source data only.

For metric mm, view vv, and scored target set 𝒰v\mathcal{U}_{v}, write

m¯v=1|𝒰v|​∑u∈𝒰v(13​∑s=13mu,v,s).\overline{m}_{v}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{U}_{v}|}\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}_{v}}\left(\frac{1}{3}\sum_{s=1}^{3}m_{u,v,s}\right). (57)

The three runs use seeds 42, 43, and 44. A domain or dataset receives one vote regardless of its task count. For cross-domain evaluation, 𝒰v\mathcal{U}_{v} contains domains with evaluation tasks and at least five available candidate capabilities in view vv. Domain–view cells with fewer than five capabilities are excluded from the macro average; their scores are not filled with zero. This eligibility rule is shared by all methods and seeds. It gives 49, 39, 49, and 44 scored domains for Natural, Semantic, Context, and Mixed, respectively. Per-target means and sample standard deviations are reported in Appendix J.2. Model fitting and selection follow Appendix G; the outer target supplies no relevance supervision for these operations.

Table 6 summarizes the overall scale of the two protocols. Tasks refer to the Natural-view evaluation population, while candidate pairs count all task–capability records in the corresponding frozen manifests.

H.2 Domain Coverage and Evaluation Eligibility

The domain roster follows the 49 ToolBench domain names listed in Tables 16–19. The Natural and Context results contain a score for every domain. Semantic has records in 42 domains but scores in 39; Mixed has records in 46 domains but scores in 44. The excluded nonempty cells contain fewer than five available candidate capabilities: Jobs, Logistics, and Monitoring in Semantic, and Energy and Storage in Mixed. The detailed tables retain their task counts and mark ranking scores with a dash. Here NN counts tasks, not capabilities. Candidate-manifest statistics cover all constructed records, whereas ranking macro averages include only eligible domains.

H.3 Candidate-Manifest Statistics

The four candidate views are constructed to probe different ranking failures. Natural preserves the original candidate distribution; Semantic introduces functionally incompatible but semantically related candidates; Context introduces candidates whose apparent support does not transfer safely to the target context; and Mixed combines the Semantic and Context hard-negative types with ordinary candidates.

Eligibility is determined separately for each view. A task is retained only when the required view-specific hard candidate can be constructed under the frozen rules. The resulting task populations may therefore differ across views. Within every dataset–view or group–view manifest, however, all methods are evaluated on exactly the same tasks and candidate sets.

Cross-dataset candidate composition.

Table 7 reports the scale and candidate-role composition of each dataset–view combination. The “Other” column contains the remaining ordinary or unclassified candidate records after positives, Semantic candidates, and Context candidates are counted.

Cross-domain candidate composition.

Table 8 aggregates the corresponding statistics over the 49 ToolBench domains. Natural and Context retain tasks from all 49 underlying domains, whereas Semantic and Mixed have candidate records in 42 and 46 domains, respectively. Ranking evaluation further requires at least five available capabilities in a domain–view cell, giving 39 scored Semantic domains and 44 scored Mixed domains. All methods use the same eligible domains within each view.

H.4 Candidate Audits

We assess candidate construction with a double-blind, two-stage audit. Two AI judges review samples from all four datasets, and two human reviewers independently audit a ToolBench sample. Assessors do not see method identities, model scores, evaluation outcomes, or one another’s judgments; human reviewers also do not see the AI decisions. Acceptance within each stage requires both assessors to approve the record. For records assessed in both stages, final acceptance requires passing both the AI and human audits. The tables report the stages separately over their respective samples. Audit labels characterize the frozen candidate manifests and are not used for training or scoring.

Cross-dataset AI construction audit.

For each dataset, two independent AI judges evaluate Semantic and Context candidates as matched task–candidate pairs and evaluate Mixed at the complete candidate-pool level. Both judges apply the same view-specific rubric for semantic relevance, functional compatibility, and contextual applicability. A pair or pool passes the AI stage only when both judges confirm that it meets the criteria of its intended view. A rejection by either judge makes the record invalid; if neither rejects it but a required judgment is indeterminate, the record is unresolved. Table 9 reports this audit across all four datasets and the three constructed candidate views.

Independent ToolBench human audit.

In the second stage, two human reviewers independently assess sampled ToolBench records using the same view-specific criteria and double-blind protocol. A record is accepted only if both reviewers approve it and it also passes the AI stage. Neither stage can compensate for failure in the other. Table 10 reports acceptance, raw human agreement, and Cohen’s κ\kappa for the four views. Agreement statistics use the independent human judgments before combining stages. Natural is retained as a reference for annotation consistency, whereas Semantic, Context, and Mixed evaluate the corresponding construction criteria.

H.5 Leakage Controls and Evaluation Boundary

All candidate manifests are frozen before evaluation and shared by all compared methods. Target-side task–capability annotations are used only to define final evaluation records and compute ranking metrics. They are never used for model training, calibration, early stopping, source-context selection, training-negative sampling, expansion ranking, or hyperparameter selection. Their use in constructing frozen evaluation labels and candidate manifests is kept separate from model development.

At inference, each method may access the task text, permitted public capability information, and the source-derived information listed in Table 14. Cross-dataset alignment may also use the unlabeled target embedding statistics specified there. The target-context identifier and target-side relevance labels are never provided as model inputs. When a source context is held out for internal selection, its observations are excluded from the source-derived profiles and statistics used to evaluate that context.

Candidate audits assess benchmark quality only and do not alter the frozen candidate sets or reported results. In expanded-library experiments, annotated target positives define the relevance boundary, while additional unjudged capabilities are treated as non-relevant. These experiments therefore measure recovery of known positives as the library grows, rather than establishing that every unannotated capability is functionally invalid.

Appendix I Implementation Details

This section provides the staged optimization protocol, principal hyperparameters, baseline adaptations, and computational environment corresponding to the implementation details summarized in the main text.

I.1 Optimization Protocol

The staged objectives, cross-fitting boundary, and nested source-only selection procedure are specified in Appendix G. This section collects numerical settings, baseline adaptations, public-input specifications, and the computational environment. Discrete hyperparameter sets below are source-only search spaces, not settings selected using the outer target.

I.2 Main Configuration

Table 11 summarizes the principal TACT configuration.

We use a frozen all-MiniLM-L6-v2 encoder and do not update its parameters during training. The task-side requirement extractor produces at most four requirements, and endpoint retrieval retains a shared set of at most four endpoints for each task–capability pair, reused across all extracted requirements and evidence channels. Endpoint-set training epochs and correction strengths are selected using source contexts.

I.3 Baseline Adaptations and Input Specifications

All baselines are adapted to the same task–capability ranking interface. Given a task and a frozen candidate set, each method produces a scalar score for every task–capability pair and ranks candidates in descending order. All methods use the same outer splits, candidate manifests, and evaluation labels. Target-side relevance labels are reserved exclusively for final evaluation.

Random assigns pseudo-random candidate scores reproducibly within each evaluation seed. Semantic Cosine encodes the same public task and capability text used by the frozen TACT anchor and ranks candidates by cosine similarity. It requires no supervised task–capability fitting.

Endpoint Schema Match is a deterministic, training-free structural baseline. Within the operation-retrieved endpoint pool, it aggregates argument-name and argument-type similarities for each endpoint and uses the maximum endpoint score for ranking. It receives no relevance labels, context identifiers, or outputs from TACT.

Logistic Ranker applies pointwise classification to compact task–capability comparison features, including semantic similarity, embedding distance, element-wise interactions, and representation norms. Pointwise MLP takes the task embedding, capability embedding, their element-wise product, and their absolute difference as input.

MultiPool pools all outer-source domains or datasets and trains one ranker on the resulting source data. It has no explicit mechanism for separating invariant compatibility from context-dependent applicability. For cross-dataset evaluation, the MultiPool variant further applies label-free transductive model-signature alignment using unlabeled target task and capability embedding statistics. It never uses target relevance labels. TACT also uses unlabeled target embedding statistics for label-free coordinate alignment, as stated in the main text; the two alignment procedures should not be conflated.

ZESRec, UniSRec, and AREAD adapt the corresponding transfer-learning ideas to task–capability ranking. ZESRec uses separate task and capability towers with source-trained capability residuals. UniSRec applies mixture-of-experts adaptors to frozen task and capability representations. AREAD combines an invariant score with a source-context-aware correction.

Re-Invoke follows the original configuration with text-bison@001 for capability-side query generation and task-side intent extraction, and textembedding-gecko@003 for dense retrieval (Chen et al., 2024). ToolDreamer uses GPT-4.1 to generate hypothetical tools and the authors’ Qwen3-8B dense and BM25 retrieval configurations (Sengupta et al., 2026). The generated thought, tool name, and description are combined with the task query (QTND), and retrieved lists are combined by reciprocal rank fusion (RRF). These retrieval configurations use public task and capability text without target relevance labels or source-side retriever fitting.

PORTS.

We use the authors’ PORTS implementation11 1 https://github.com/disi-unibo-nlp/ports with its original backbone and encoder configurations (Molfetta et al., 2025). The frozen preference models are Codestral-22B-v0.1, Llama-3-8B, and Llama-3-Groq-8B-Tool-Use; the retriever encoders are RoBERTa-base and BGE-base. The adaptation maps task–capability records to the authors’ retrieval interface and fits the retriever with preference supervision from outer-source records. Model selection also uses source data only. Results use seeds 42, 43, and 44.

Baseline configurations.

Table 12 reports model architectures and optimization settings. Pointwise MLP, ZESRec, UniSRec, AREAD, PORTS, and MultiPool use outer-source training data. The table also specifies the Logistic Ranker control. Generation-enhanced retrievers use the fixed configurations below.

Generation settings and prompts.

Table 13 summarizes the generation and retrieval configurations. The generation prompts are given below. In Re-Invoke, {tool_document} is the normalized public capability text; no separate endpoint or parameter-schema columns are appended.

Re-Invoke tool-side prompt.

Suppose you are an assistant and you have access to the following API to answer user’s queries. You are provided with a tool and its available API function including the description and parameters. Your task is to generate a possible user query that can be handled by the API. You must include the input parameters required in the API call. Please be creative and generate random but specific information for the required parameters. Now you are given the API documentation below: {tool_document} Please generate a user query that you will need to call this tool. Note the generated query should be complex enough to describe the scenarios that you will need to call the provided API to address them. The relevant query is: The ten generated queries are serialized as Documentation: {skill_text} Query: {synthetic_query}. Their textembedding-gecko@003 vectors are averaged to represent the augmented capability document. Multiple task intents are fused by the maximum lexicographic (reversed rank,similarity)(\text{reversed rank},\text{similarity}) tuple.

Re-Invoke task-side intent prompt.

**Instructions** Suppose you are a query analyzer and your task is to extract the underlying user intents from the input query. You should preserve all the underlying user request and the extracted user intents should be easily understood without extra context information. You should carefully read the given user query to understand its different intents. Then identify what are the specific intents. Each individual intent should be separated by a newline. Here are some examples of how you should solve the task. Example Query: I’m planning to travel to Paris next weekend to visit my family, could you help me book a round trip flight ticket? I want to fly in economy class. Intent: book a round-trip flight ticket in economy class to Paris next weekend Query: I’m a potential buyer looking for a condominium in the city of Miami. I am specifically interested in properties that have a minimum of two bathrooms. It should have walkable distance to the grocery stores. Intent: buy a real estate in Miami with a minimum of two bathrooms and walkable distance to the grocery stores Query: I want to learn Spanish by talking to the native speakers at any time. Additionally, can you recommend some interesting books, preferably fictions, so that I can learn by reading? Also include the websites that I can buy them. Intent: learn Spanish by talking to the native speakers recommend fictions to learn Spanish by reading suggest the websites to buy Spanish fictions **Begin!** Query: {user_query} Intent:

ToolDreamer prompt.

You are a tool-crafting assistant. Your goal is to design a set of hypothetical tools that can collectively solve a given user query. These tools behave like independent, stateless functions and have access to all relevant structured data needed to complete their task. No external internet access is assumed. High-Level Strategy 1. Break down the query into distinct, logically separable subtasks. 2. For each subtask, propose exactly one tool that performs only that task. 3. Tools must be modular, reusable, and generic where possible (e.g., ’getPopulationData’). If a subtask clearly requires specialized or scoped logic (e.g., region-specific), it’s acceptable to use a specialized tool, but its name must reflect its limited scope (e.g., ’weatherAPI_California’, ’fetchStockData_TechSector’). 4. All tools must be: - Implementation-agnostic - Independent - Named consistently using ’camelCase’ or ’snake_case’ 5. Every query must result in at least one tool being proposed. Output Format For each tool, respond using the following format: Thought: [Explain why this tool is necessary and what subtask it addresses] Tool Name: [Concise and consistent tool name] Tool Description: [Describe what this tool does in one or two sentences, avoiding implementation details] Example User Query: What is the average temperature in San Francisco? Assistant Response: Thought: To answer this query, we need to retrieve historical and/or current temperature data for a specific location in California. Tool Name: weatherAPI_California Tool Description: Retrieves current and historical temperature data for locations in California. Additional Tips - Do not suggest tool pipelines or combine subtasks into a single tool. - If the query involves data transformation (e.g., averaging, filtering, ranking), propose a separate tool for that. - Treat each tool as stateless and composable. User Query: {user_query} Assistant Response: Each parsed tool is serialized into the following fields for retrieval:

Question: {original_query} Thoughts: {thought} Tool Name: {name} Tool Description: {description} The retrieval configurations use Qwen3-8B dense embeddings and BM25 scores. Ranked lists from the hypothetical tools are combined with RRF, and direct-query retrieval supplies candidates outside their union and the fallback when generation or parsing fails.

Input parity.

Table 14 summarizes the information available to representative comparison methods. In particular, Endpoint Schema Match is given exactly the same public endpoint-operation and argument-name/type schema evidence as TACT. Therefore, the comparison controls for access to public endpoint/schema evidence rather than advantages from additional schema inputs. The main-paper w/o Functional ablation removes Functional Validation, while w/o Context removes Contextual Validation. TACT further decomposes the task into local requirements, requires supporting evidence to be composed within the same endpoint, imposes capacity-constrained requirement–endpoint matching, and calibrates the resulting evidence using structural reliability and bounded corrections. TACT additionally uses source-derived capability profiles in its contextual applicability branch; these profiles are not used by Endpoint Schema Match.

All trainable baselines—Logistic Ranker, Pointwise MLP, ZESRec, UniSRec, AREAD, PORTS, and MultiPool—use outer-source training data only. Cross-dataset MultiPool additionally uses unlabeled target embedding statistics for label-free transductive model-signature alignment. Cross-dataset TACT uses unlabeled target embedding statistics only for label-free coordinate alignment. Neither method uses target relevance labels for these alignment operations. Frozen, structural, and generation-based retrievers require no supervised task–capability fitting. PORTS additionally uses frozen-LLM preference supervision on source records.

I.4 Computational Environment

Local representation extraction, model training, and capability ranking are conducted on a server equipped with three NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, each with 95 GB of memory. The software environment uses Python 3.11.15, PyTorch 2.10.0 with CUDA 12.8, and cuDNN 9.10.2. Unless otherwise specified, experiments are repeated with random seeds 42, 43, and 44.

The downstream cached-execution environment is separated from the local ranking experiments. StableToolBench tool calls are executed through the local MirrorAPI-Cache service, whereas the agent backbones and blinded judge are accessed through remote model endpoints. Because the hardware underlying these remote endpoints is neither controlled nor observable, we report their model identifiers and inference settings rather than assigning them the local GPU configuration.

A dash marks a cell excluded from ranking evaluation because it has no tasks or fewer than five available candidate capabilities; it is never treated as zero. Scores are reported for 49, 39, 49, and 44 domains in Natural, Semantic, Context, and Mixed, respectively. The capability-count rule excludes three Semantic cells with positive task counts (Jobs: 1; Logistics: 3; Monitoring: 1) and two Mixed cells (Energy: 4; Storage: 2). These numbers are task counts; the other excluded cells have N=0N=0.

Table 21 gives equal-weight means over scored targets, calculated from the displayed four-decimal cell means. The domain means agree with the Full-model cross-domain results in Table 1, up to rounding of the per-target cells. Individual held-out domains are the aggregation units. The held-out-group experiment in Appendix J.3 provides a separate comparison using five predefined groups.

Dataset-level results.

Table 20 reports all four held-out datasets in every view. Table 21 gives their equal-target means. These agree with the Full-model cross-dataset results in Table 1 within the rounding precision of the displayed target and aggregate means. Aggregation of rounded target cells may differ slightly from aggregation before rounding.

The standard deviation of a target-macro score cannot be recovered by averaging the individual target standard deviations. It requires the target scores for each seed; no macro standard deviation is reconstructed here.

J.3 Supplementary Held-Out-Group Results

This supplementary experiment holds out one of five predefined ToolBench domain groups, using the remaining four groups as sources. Table 22 specifies the partition of all 49 domains. Training, calibration, and model selection remain source-only.

Table 23 reports means and sample standard deviations in paired rows over seeds 42, 43, and 44. This group-held-out experiment complements the individual held-out-domain evaluation in Appendix J.2. Comparisons between methods are made within each protocol; differences between the group-held-out and domain-held-out aggregates are not estimates of a method gain.

Appendix K Downstream Cached Execution Details

K.1 Solvability Filtering and Frozen Policies

We evaluate whether frozen capability rankings improve downstream tool execution using the StableToolBench MirrorAPI-Cache environment. A query is declared solvable before any ranking policy is evaluated only when its annotated capability is present in the frozen library, at least one permitted public endpoint can be instantiated from the available schema, and the endpoint has a valid MirrorAPI-Cache response without requiring authentication, a write operation, or a live external side effect. The final evaluation contains 120 such queries sampled from 24 ToolBench domains, with five tasks per domain. Table 24 reports the frozen pre-evaluation filtering counts.

For each task, we evaluate five paired capability-selection policies: no tools, Semantic Cosine Top-5, MultiPool Top-5, Re-Invoke Top-5, and full-model Top-5. All ranking policies operate over the complete library of 3,442 capabilities, and their configurations are selected from source domains only, without target relevance labels or target-domain tuning.

K.2 Cached Execution Setting

Recommended capabilities are converted into callable endpoints using only the user query, public capability documentation, and public endpoint schemas. Only read-only GET and HEAD endpoints are allowed, with at most 20 endpoints per case, eight endpoints per capability, eight agent turns, and four parallel tool calls per turn. Tool calls are executed through the local StableToolBench MirrorAPI-Cache service, while agent and judge models are accessed through remote LLM endpoints. Thus, the experiment evaluates virtual StableToolBench API execution rather than live external API services.

K.3 Agents, Judging, and Paired Comparisons

Four agent backbones are evaluated: GPT-5.6 Terra, Grok-4.5, Claude Sonnet 5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro. Each agent processes all 120×5=600120\times 5=600 task–policy cases using temperature zero and automatic function calling, producing 120×5×4=2,400120\times 5\times 4=2{,}400 task–policy–backbone cases in total. A blinded GPT-5.6-sol judge receives only the user request, final answer, and tool observations; policy identities, ranking scores, recommended capabilities, backend information, and gold annotations are hidden. The primary metric is execution completion rate, with task-cluster bootstrap intervals, and paired exact McNemar tests used for uncertainty analysis; results appear in Table 25.

Appendix L Scaling and Evidence Availability Details

L.1 Candidate-Library Scaling

Table 3 expands the cross-domain ToolBench candidate library from the base candidate sets to 100, 500, and all 3,442 capabilities. Pool sizes count all candidates, including positives, rather than only newly added candidates.

For cross-dataset scaling, let |𝒞d||\mathcal{C}_{d}| denote the number of available capabilities in target dataset dd. A nominal pool size BB uses min⁡(B,|𝒞d|)\min(B,|\mathcal{C}_{d}|) candidates; if the target library contains fewer than 100 or 500 capabilities, the corresponding setting uses the entire available library. Full always denotes the complete target library. Thus, nominal sizes can coincide with Full for smaller datasets. Seeds are averaged within targets, followed by an equal-target macro average over ToolBench, TaskBench, MetaTool, and APIBench.

At Full scale, TACT exceeds Semantic Cosine in cross-dataset NDCG@5 by 0.0378, 0.0478, 0.0572, and 0.0469 on Natural, Semantic, Context, and Mixed, respectively. The equal-view averages are 0.4475 for TACT and 0.4001 for Semantic Cosine, a difference of 0.0474. These results describe recovery of annotated positives from expanded libraries and do not imply a smaller absolute Base-to-Full decline.

L.2 Fixed-Checkpoint Source-Evidence Diagnostic

The source-evidence intervention uses the Full checkpoints from the primary ranking experiment under the corresponding transfer protocol. The outer splits, selected parameters, calibration, and candidate pools are fixed. Checkpoints and calibration are shared across Natural, Semantic, Context, and Mixed. Only the fraction of retained source associations changes; the model is not retrained or reselected for an evidence level.

At each level, Full incorporates all available source evidence, whereas Fixed-Checkpoint Functional Fallback excludes the contextual contribution while keeping the remaining score components unchanged. When no source evidence is available, the two settings become identical. Cross-domain results are macro-averaged over the same eligible target domains as in the primary ranking experiment, while cross-dataset results are macro-averaged across the four target datasets.

This intervention measures the contribution of contextual correction within the fitted Full model. The RQ2 w/o Context ablation instead trains and selects a separate model without that branch. The former is a fixed-checkpoint diagnostic; the latter is an independently trained branch ablation.

L.3 Closed-World Evaluation Boundary

Expanded pools retain the frozen relevance boundary: annotated positives are relevant and additional unjudged capabilities are treated as non-relevant. Scaling measures recovery of known positives, not the incompatibility of every unannotated capability. Target labels define evaluation sets and final metrics; they are not used for training, selection, expansion ranking, or evidence interventions.
